title: Why every Wikimedian should be a toolmaker

AI is not magic, but consensus building is. Notes on Wikimedia’s next 25 years, after Wikimania 2026.

This article is ~3,000 words and will take you around 15 minutes to read.

In 1997 Garry Kasparov lost a chess match against Deep Blue, a chess computer built by IBM. It was the first time a reigning world chess champion lost to a computer.

In the media it was framed as ‘man versus machine’. But Feng-hsiung Hsu, the main designer of Deep Blue, later wrote that this assumption was wrong. He saw the match as one type of human versus another. Human as performer (Kasparov) versus human as toolmaker (the Deep Blue team).

I’ve been thinking a lot about that match since I’ve returned last week from Paris where I attended Wikimania: the world’s largest gathering of Wikimedians (people who write Wikipedia and its siblings). With 1,250 people attending in person and over 2,000 online we celebrated Wikipedia having its 25th birthday this year with five intense days of talks, workshops and of course many, many meetings and conversations with Wikimedians from all around the world.

One question was woven throughout virtually every session and conversation: in a world where AI is reshaping both the digital and physical world, how do we as a community deal with it? As Christophe Henner wrote earlier this year, AI is not a tool but a paradigm shift. How do we make sure we continue being relevant in the next 25 years?

I’ve been a Wikimedian for 21 years and a developer. The last few years I’ve used AI in many of my projects. So I have some thoughts about this.

Earlier this year I hosted two workshops during the Wikimedia Hackathon in Milan about this question which resulted in this blogpost. At Wikimania I repeated this workshop during the Wiki AI Preconference.

After the three workshops i organized and five days of Wikimania one thing for me is clear: just as Kasparov was playing against other humans and not a machine we’re competing against other humans who have figured out how to be better at some of the things we do.

What this means? We should become better toolmakers as well.

Unsure of what all the terms in this article mean? Click here to read a glossary of terms.
  • The projects refer to the Wikimedia projects (Wikipedia, Wikidata, Wikimedia Commons, etc.).
  • The community, movement or Wikimedians are the people who work on those projects, both in a hired capacity (e.g. from the Wikimedia Foundation or affiliates) or as volunteers.
  • The foundation or the WMF refers to the Wikimedia Foundation, the supporting organization which provides the hosting and technical infrastructure for the Wikimedia projects.
  • The affiliates refer to the local Wikimedia chapters (e.g. Wikimedia Netherlands) and user groups (e.g. LGBT+ User Group).
  • LLMs are ‘large language models’, so ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.
  • Frontier models are the AI models that power the most well-known LLM chatbots listed above.
  • Local models are models that run on your own computer instead of in the cloud. These are usually less capable than frontier models, but can be good enough for specific tasks. More capable local models need a lot of RAM; 16GB is usually the bare minimum.
  • Open weight models can be downloaded for free and can run on your own computer (compared to many frontier models which are closed). However, some of the more capable models can require so much RAM that they still run in the cloud (e.g. DeepSeek V4 Pro needs 862GB of RAM).
  • Inference is generating content using an LLM, e.g. writing code using an LLM chatbot.
  • Tokens are the basic unit an LLM takes as input and produces as output. Most models are priced based on tokens, and better models tend to cost more per token.
  • Open licenses are the conditions under which the content on the Wikimedia projects is available. Creative Commons BY-SA and Zero are the most popular ones. An open license means you can reuse the content for most purposes for free, even commercially.
  • Markdown is an important input/output format for LLMs. It’s a plain text format that provides a simple syntax that translates to HTML. E.g. text *between asterisks* is rendered in italics.

Three challenges

As a movement we face three major challenges:

1. Fewer humans

Our community is dependent on people visiting our projects. Because we need new editors, who start out as readers. And we need donations. The projects are funded mostly by small donations of readers who pass by and donate a small amount. If that source dries up because people consume Wikipedia content via an LLM or Google’s ‘AI Overview’ we have a problem.

Declining readership is a real trend that has been noted by the Wikimedia Foundation. It’s interesting that some comparable projects, like OpenStreetMap, are not so dependent on readership and have always focused more on being a data source instead of a destination. So maybe this is less of an issue than we think. But for now, I would say that we should err on the side of caution and see declining readership as a serious issue.

One other consequence of less humans on our projects is that the distance between consumers of our content and the people who produce it will get even bigger. It has always been an issue to explain to people that there are actual, breathing humans writing those articles together. LLMs might condition people into thinking that Wikipedia is just a bunch of AI bots writing articles. Another reason why they might be hesitant to donate or become an editor.

2. More robots

While humans are visiting our projects less and less, more and more robots appear. Many of those robots are scrapers, harvesting our data at unsustainable speeds. This has put a giant strain on our infrastructure. It feels like a lose-lose situation. Wikimedia provides one of the most important data sources for LLMs, in return we get a barrage of scraping bots, and we need to invest more in our infrastructure.

3. More slop

AI-generated articles are an issue as well. Apart from the regular vandalism that we have always had, now we need to deal with seemingly well-written articles that turn out to be generated by LLMs.

We have always included machine generated content (some Wikipedias are even written almost entirely with it), the question is where to draw the line in including AI-generated content.

This is not just an internal problem. Wikipedia is reliant on references to write verifiable articles. If the internet turns into a cesspool of AI slop it becomes harder and harder to find reliable sources.

Internal struggles

There are also internal issues that might weaken our position.

One important reason for organizing my Milan workshop was that not all voices in the movement were heard. Should we even use AI, or maybe ban the use of LLMs and coding agents altogether? Especially young people can have a very negative opinion on any usage of AI at all. If parts of our community feel left out of this discussion it might lead to internal polarization.

There are more than enough reasons to be skeptical of or opposed to the use of AI. The earlier mentioned lack of reciprocity from the companies who’ve been using our data, energy consumption, the atrocious working conditions in which some models have been ‘finetuned’, jobs getting lost, AI powering military ‘killer drones’, questionable government ties and many many more.

However, there was surprisingly little discussion in Paris about this subject. Maybe people have simply accepted that we’ll have a future where AI is an essential technology? Or maybe they haven’t, but they didn’t speak up? I don’t know, but i would love to read or hear more from those folks.

Another issue is the delicate balance within the movement between volunteers, affiliates and the foundation. The relationship between those three factions is complicated and at times very tense. See for example the proposed new rules concerning board member eligibility, updates to the structure of funding affiliates and the actions (or rather lack thereof) from the Foundation in relation to the Wiki Workers United solidarity union. Important decisions could be delayed and hampered by internal debate and discussions.

Humans must stay responsible

Let’s get back to the ‘man as performer vs man as toolmaker’ narrative.

If we agree on the notion that the significant shift in the world is not ‘machines are taking over’, but ‘machines controlled by humans are taking over’, it also makes sense that humans must stay responsible for the actions of the machines they build and use.

That might seem obvious, but it’s not. People who used to depend on programmers can now suddenly do many things themselves. This might feel like magic. Suddenly they’re able to write a complicated Excel formula! Or vibecode a little app for the paperwork they previously had to hire a company for!

Of course, most developers and technically skilled people know that computers aren’t magic and are very aware of the shortcomings. When you write code (by hand or using a coding agent) that accidentally deletes the production database of your company, “it’s the machine that did it” isn’t an excuse your manager will accept. And even in the age of coding agents, maintaining complicated software infrastructure is still hard work.

However, right now all over the world companies are firing their development teams and replacing them with AI agents, expecting everything will be the same, but cheaper. Of course, it’s not.

It seems that for some people, it takes firing their developers to discover that machines are not the same as people, and code isn’t magic.

Leveraging our biggest strengths

Code and AI aren’t magic. And I think that we, as Wikimedians, are particularly well-placed to explain and show how the ‘magic’ works. Just as Wikipedia articles explain that things are usually a lot more complicated than you think.

And that isn’t the only strength that we have. Wikimedia may be the David to big tech’s Goliath, but we often underestimate our own strengths.

Even though the big tech companies that make the major LLMs have a seemingly limitless supply of money, they lack one thing that our community has in spades: trust and reliability. Wikimedians are fervent nitpickers, making sure statements are properly referenced and factually accurate. Even though LLMs tend to get many things right (because they have been trained on sources like Wikipedia) they also get many things wrong. Even if Google’s “AI overview” is wrong “only” 10% of the time, that means millions of people get wrong answers every day.

Wikipedia is the critical data set used in most LLMs. We need to figure out how we can take advantage of that. Our open licenses are both one of our biggest strengths and weaknesses. It’s very hard to make big tech pony up for our data in a capitalist world because they already got it for free. However, Wikimedia data is valuable because it’s one of the few high quality human-generated data sets (and probably less destructive than AI companies destroying print books to train their models).

Another strength is that we are non-personalized. Folks using social media to get their news stay in their bubble, fed only the things that suit their taste. But on Wikipedia everyone reads the same article. Us not providing a ‘personalized reading experience’ is a feature, not a bug.

We have the moral upper hand when we’re talking about big tech vs Wikimedia. Efforts like Grokipedia, which is fully AI-generated, fail because there are no humans to check on articles. Grokipedia cited the Kremlin as a prominent source on the invasion of Ukraine because they’re using AI models. A Wikimedian would spot that immediately.

AI is not magic, but you know what is? Consensus building with humans.

Every Wikimedian should be a toolmaker

We have identified our strengths. Now, how should we use them?

It’s tempting to take a defensive stance against the big tech companies, and maybe even AI in general. But it’s better to play offense than defense. Big tech also doesn’t know what’s going to happen. It’s better if we try to invent the future ourselves instead of waiting around until something happens.

That means that right now we should focus on experiment over decisions. It’s better to do a lot of small experiments instead of making large-scale long-term bets. We should act deliberately, not emotionally, in the way Wikimedians do best: with nuance, knowledge and a scientific, objective look. And because of that we might be able to apply new technologies in a meaningful and useful way instead of jumping on the AI hype wagon and trying to cram AI into everything.

Another reason why we should experiment now is because the current situation is not going to last forever. Using LLMs today can be dirt cheap because of the influx of venture capital. If something like Claude Opus or Fable is too expensive, DeepSeek v4-flash is almost as capable and can generate millions of tokens for next to nothing. To put that into perspective: the total codebase of MediaWiki with all extensions is roughly 3 million lines of code. An amount of code like that could be generated by this model for about 11 dollars.

It’s very unlikely the situation will remain like this. The AI bubble will burst at some point in the near future, and then usage will suddenly be a lot more expensive. This also means that we need to prepare for that, and make sure that the tools we build don’t rely on AI models or can use simpler, self-hosted ones.

It also gives us a great opportunity. As mentioned, people who can’t code suddenly can code now. And people who used to code in the past may rediscover their joy of coding again. They should get accustomed to the best practices that are evolving right now.

Want to know what those best practices are? Click here to find out.
  1. Using a coding agent. Claude Code is the most well-known but there are many capable open source alternatives as well like pi.dev and Hermes.
  2. Be aware of the dangers. A coding agent can be run in ‘yolo mode‘, which means it has unrestricted access to your machine, up to and including deleting files by accident. You should either be careful in giving permissions or use a “harness” to restrict access to your system.
  3. Use skills. Skills are text files written in Markdown that instruct a LLM about a specific task like ‘connecting to the Wikidata API’ or ‘finding pageview metrics on Wikipedia articles’.
  4. Try out different models. Obviously everyone should try the frontier models, but it’s interesting, if only for the exercise, to try out a locally hosted or open weights model.
  5. Use best practices. One thing that has always been very hard in software development is making sure people follow best practices. This includes things like unit tests and documentation, but it also includes providing your app in different languages (internationalization or ‘i18n’) and making sure it’s accessible (‘a11y’). With coding agents this becomes much easier. They don’t complain about writing documentation!

The Wikimedia Foundation announced that they are experimenting with hosting some open weights models on their LiftWing infrastructure. Currently, this includes the relatively modest Qwen 3-14B and 3.6-27B models. Hopefully those models will be more capable in future.

Of course, the answer to “what should we do” is a little bit more nuanced than just “build lots of tools”. We already have over 4,000 tools, many of them unmaintained and/or broken. We don’t want to get an overload of new tools that are then unmaintained and no longer used. We might need to set expectations higher for the tools we use, or be more vigilant in deprecating and removing old ones.

Using AI for Wikimedia doesn’t mean writing articles

So if every Wikimedian builds tools, what do we build? When talking about generative AI the first thing that comes to mind is ‘writing articles’, but that’s probably one of the least useful applications. And just as Wikimedians are doing many more things apart from writing Wikipedia articles, AI can be used for many different applications as well.

I liked how Andrew Lih talked about a ‘friction matrix‘ for Wiki AI tools. Low/high burden on one axis (for humans) and low/high impact on the other. It’s interesting to look at tools that have high impact, but a low burden. This means the many, many tedious repetitive tasks done by Wikimedians that can be replaced or at least simplified by building new AI-assisted tools.

A great example of this was the PoliLoom tool showed by Ada Homolova and Johan Schuijt. It allows Wikipedia-sourced facts about politicians to be imported into their Wikidata items. This includes data points like place of birth and political position. Using AI, they analyzed Wikipedia articles to highlight sentences (e.g. ‘Jane Doe was born in Paris’) and prepare the appropriate Wikidata edit (e.g. Jane Doe -> Born in Paris). A human editor is always required to verify the proposed edit. A good example of a task humans can do, but AI accelerates.

Another obvious use case for AI-tools is helping smaller-language communities. There are almost 350 Wikipedia language editions. For many of them, Wikipedia is the only major reference work in that language. AI tools could help the limited number of volunteers who work on those editions to maintain their projects.

Teaming up

Of course, we as Wikimedians, are not alone in this journey. We’ve always had many friends who share our values about open access to data, verifiability and shepherding the open web. This includes parties like the Internet Archive, Creative Commons, OpenStreetMap and many others. It only makes sense to team up with those parties and collectively agree on what steps we should take to make sure the internet remains true to our vision.

Therefore it’s good to see initiatives like Mosaic, which brings together many different ‘commons’-related parties, not least because the possibilities for knowledge and cultural institutions like galleries, libraries, archives and museums (GLAMs) are tremendous. One can only imagine a future in which relevant data is shared easily by GLAMs to Wikimedia using new AI-powered tools.

One suggestion for a new tool I loved was Audrey Tang‘s idea about an ‘LLM edit button’. Every editor started by discovering the ‘edit’ button at some point at the top of every Wikipedia article. With the move from consuming Wikimedia content from the web to LLMs we lack that button. What would an ‘edit’ button look like in the age of AI?

Together we can create an alternative to the commercial closed web dominated by big tech. One where humans stay in control and build a world in which every single human being can freely share in the sum of all knowledge.

Happy birthday Wikipedia!

Notes and sources

In the interest of brevity and reading clarity I’m not sourcing every single statement and observation here. Many of the statements and sentiments were expressed multiple times by different people. I’m just trying to paraphrase.

I used the Claude Opus 5 and Gemma 4 12B models for spelling and grammar corrections, smoothing clunky sentences and general tips and feedback. 99% of the text you’ve read was written by a human.

  • Wayback Machine Labs
  • Andrew Lih’s Wikimedia AI skills
  • Open-weight LLMs hosted on Wikimedia’s infrastructure (LiftWing)
  • What is an AI harness?

The Wikimedia Foundation announced that they are experimenting with hosting some open weights models on their LiftWing infrastructure. Currently, this includes the relatively modest Qwen 3-14B and 3.6-27B models. Hopefully those models will be more capable in future. Of course, the answer to “what should we do” is a little bit more nuanced than just “build lots of tools”. We already have over 4,000 tools, many of them unmaintained and/or broken. We don’t want to get an overload of new tools that are then unmaintained and no longer used. We might need to set expectations higher for the tools we use, or be more vigilant in deprecating and removing old ones. Using AI for Wikimedia doesn’t mean writing articles So if every Wikimedian builds tools, what do we build? When talking about generative AI the first thing that comes to mind is ‘writing articles’, but that’s probably one of the least useful applications. And just as Wikimedians are doing many more things apart from writing Wikipedia articles, AI can be used for many different applications as well. I liked how Andrew Lih talked about a ‘friction matrix‘ for Wiki AI tools. Low/high burden on one axis (for humans) and low/high impact on the other. It’s interesting to look at tools that have high impact, but a low burden. This means the many, many tedious repetitive tasks done by Wikimedians that can be replaced or at least simplified by building new AI-assisted tools. A great example of this was the PoliLoom tool showed by Ada Homolova and Johan Schuijt. It allows Wikipedia-sourced facts about politicians to be imported into their Wikidata items. This includes data points like place of birth and political position. Using AI, they analyzed Wikipedia articles to highlight sentences (e.g. ‘Jane Doe was born in Paris’) and prepare the appropriate Wikidata edit (e.g. Jane Doe -> Born in Paris). A human editor is always required to verify the proposed edit. A good example of a task humans can do, but AI accelerates. Another obvious use case for AI-tools is helping smaller-language communities. There are almost 350 Wikipedia language editions. For many of them, Wikipedia is the only major reference work in that language. AI tools could help the limited number of volunteers who work on those editions to maintain their projects. Teaming up Of course, we as Wikimedians, are not alone in this journey. We’ve always had many friends who share our values about open access to data, verifiability and shepherding the open web. This includes parties like the Internet Archive, Creative Commons, OpenStreetMap and many others. It only makes sense to team up with those parties and collectively agree on what steps we should take to make sure the internet remains true to our vision. Therefore it’s good to see initiatives like Mosaic, which brings together many different ‘commons’-related parties, not least because the possibilities for knowledge and cultural institutions like galleries, libraries, archives and museums (GLAMs) are tremendous. One can only imagine a future in which relevant data is shared easily by GLAMs to Wikimedia using new AI-powered tools. One suggestion for a new tool I loved was Audrey Tang‘s idea about an ‘LLM edit button’. Every editor started by discovering the ‘edit’ button at some point at the top of every Wikipedia article. With the move from consuming Wikimedia content from the web to LLMs we lack that button. What would an ‘edit’ button look like in the age of AI? Together we can create an alternative to the commercial closed web dominated by big tech. One where humans stay in control and build a world in which every single human being can freely share in the sum of all knowledge. Happy birthday Wikipedia! Notes and sources In the interest of brevity and reading clarity I’m not sourcing every single statement and observation here. Many of the statements and sentiments were expressed multiple times by different people. I’m just trying to paraphrase. I used the Claude Opus 5 and Gemma 4 12B models for spelling and grammar corrections, smoothing clunky sentences and general tips and feedback. 99% of the text you’ve read was written by a human. blocks.html_en: 1. Fewer humans

sentences.en: We have always included machine generated content (some Wikipedias are even written almost entirely with it), the question is where to draw the line in including AI-generated content.
sentences.zh: 我们一直都包含机器生成的内容（一些维基百科甚至几乎完全用机器生成的内容编写），问题是在包含人工智能生成的内容方面划清界限。

blocks.html_en: This is not just an internal problem. Wikipedia is reliant on references to write verifiable articles. If the internet turns into a cesspool of AI slop it becomes harder and harder to find reliable sources.

sentences.en: This is not just an internal problem.
sentences.zh: 这不仅仅是一个内部问题。

sentences.en: Wikipedia is reliant on references to write verifiable articles.
sentences.zh: 维基百科依赖参考文献来撰写可验证的文章。

sentences.en: If the internet turns into a cesspool of AI slop it becomes harder and harder to find reliable sources.
sentences.zh: 如果互联网变成了人工智能污水的污水池，那么找到可靠的来源就会变得越来越难。

blocks.html_en: Internal struggles

sentences.en: Internal struggles
sentences.zh: 内部斗争

blocks.html_en: There are also internal issues that might weaken our position.

sentences.en: There are also internal issues that might weaken our position.
sentences.zh: 还有一些内部问题可能会削弱我们的地位。

blocks.html_en: One important reason for organizing my Milan workshop was that not all voices in the movement were heard. Should we even use AI, or maybe ban the use of LLMs and coding agents altogether? Especially young people can have a very negative opinion on any usage of AI at all. If parts of our community feel left out of this discussion it might lead to internal polarization.

sentences.en: One important reason for organizing my Milan workshop was that not all voices in the movement were heard.
sentences.zh: 组织米兰研讨会的一个重要原因是，并非运动中的所有声音都被听到。

sentences.en: Should we even use AI, or maybe ban the use of LLMs and coding agents altogether?
sentences.zh: 我们是否应该使用人工智能，或者完全禁止使用法学硕士和编码代理？

sentences.en: Especially young people can have a very negative opinion on any usage of AI at all.
sentences.zh: 尤其是年轻人可能会对人工智能的任何使用持非常负面的看法。

sentences.en: If parts of our community feel left out of this discussion it might lead to internal polarization.
sentences.zh: 如果我们社区的部分人感觉被排除在这场讨论之外，可能会导致内部两极分化。

blocks.html_en: There are more than enough reasons to be skeptical of or opposed to the use of AI. The earlier mentioned lack of reciprocity from the companies who’ve been using our data, energy consumption, the atrocious working conditions in which some models have been ‘finetuned’, jobs getting lost, AI powering military ‘killer drones’, questionable government ties and many many more.

sentences.en: There are more than enough reasons to be skeptical of or opposed to the use of AI.
sentences.zh: 有足够的理由怀疑或反对人工智能的使用。

sentences.en: The earlier mentioned lack of reciprocity from the companies who’ve been using our data, energy consumption, the atrocious working conditions in which some models have been ‘finetuned’, jobs getting lost, AI powering military ‘killer drones’, questionable government ties and many many more.
sentences.zh: 前面提到的问题包括使用我们数据的公司缺乏互惠、能源消耗、某些模型被“微调”的恶劣工作条件、工作岗位流失、人工智能为军事“杀手无人机”提供动力、可疑的政府关系等等。

blocks.html_en: However, there was surprisingly little discussion in Paris about this subject. Maybe people have simply accepted that we’ll have a future where AI is an essential technology? Or maybe they haven’t, but they didn’t speak up? I don’t know, but i would love to read or hear more from those folks.

sentences.en: However, there was surprisingly little discussion in Paris about this subject.
sentences.zh: 然而，令人惊讶的是，巴黎关于这个话题的讨论却很少。

sentences.en: Maybe people have simply accepted that we’ll have a future where AI is an essential technology?
sentences.zh: 也许人们已经简单地接受了人工智能将成为一项重要技术的未来？

sentences.en: Or maybe they haven’t, but they didn’t speak up?
sentences.zh: 或者也许他们没有，但他们没有说话？

sentences.en: I don’t know, but i would love to read or hear more from those folks.
sentences.zh: 我不知道，但我很想阅读或听到这些人的更多信息。

blocks.html_en: Another issue is the delicate balance within the movement between volunteers, affiliates and the foundation. The relationship between those three factions is complicated and at times very tense. See for example the proposed new rules concerning board member eligibility, updates to the structure of funding affiliates and the actions (or rather lack thereof) from the Foundation in relation to the Wiki Workers United solidarity union. Important decisions could be delayed and hampered by internal debate and discussions.

sentences.en: Another issue is the delicate balance within the movement between volunteers, affiliates and the foundation.
sentences.zh: 另一个问题是志愿者、附属机构和基金会之间运动中的微妙平衡。

sentences.en: The relationship between those three factions is complicated and at times very tense.
sentences.zh: 这三个派系之间的关系很复杂，有时甚至非常紧张。

sentences.en: See for example the proposed new rules concerning board member eligibility, updates to the structure of funding affiliates and the actions (or rather lack thereof) from the Foundation in relation to the Wiki Workers United solidarity union.
sentences.zh: 例如，请参阅有关董事会成员资格的拟议新规则、资助附属机构的结构更新以及基金会与维基工人联合团结工会相关的行动（或者更确切地说缺乏行动）。

sentences.en: Important decisions could be delayed and hampered by internal debate and discussions.
sentences.zh: 重要的决定可能会因内部辩论和讨论而被推迟和阻碍。

blocks.html_en: Humans must stay responsible

sentences.en: Humans must stay responsible
sentences.zh: 人类必须承担责任

blocks.html_en: Let’s get back to the ‘man as performer vs man as toolmaker’ narrative.

sentences.en: Let’s get back to the ‘man as performer vs man as toolmaker’ narrative.
sentences.zh: 让我们回到“人作为表演者与人作为工具制造者”的叙述。

blocks.html_en: If we agree on the notion that the significant shift in the world is not ‘machines are taking over’, but ‘machines controlled by humans are taking over’, it also makes sense that humans must stay responsible for the actions of the machines they build and use.

sentences.en: If we agree on the notion that the significant shift in the world is not ‘machines are taking over’, but ‘machines controlled by humans are taking over’, it also makes sense that humans must stay responsible for the actions of the machines they build and use.
sentences.zh: 如果我们同意世界上的重大转变不是“机器正在接管”，而是“人类控制的机器正在接管”，那么人类必须对他们建造和使用的机器的行为负责也是有道理的。

blocks.html_en: That might seem obvious, but it’s not. People who used to depend on programmers can now suddenly do many things themselves. This might feel like magic. Suddenly they’re able to write a complicated Excel formula! Or vibecode a little app for the paperwork they previously had to hire a company for!

sentences.en: That might seem obvious, but it’s not.
sentences.zh: 这似乎是显而易见的，但事实并非如此。

sentences.en: People who used to depend on programmers can now suddenly do many things themselves.
sentences.zh: 以前依赖程序员的人们现在突然可以自己做很多事情了。

sentences.en: This might feel like magic.
sentences.zh: 这可能感觉就像魔法一样。

sentences.en: Suddenly they’re able to write a complicated Excel formula!
sentences.zh: 突然间，他们能够编写复杂的 Excel 公式！

sentences.en: Or vibecode a little app for the paperwork they previously had to hire a company for!
sentences.zh: 或者，vibecode 是一个小应用程序，用于处理他们以前必须雇用一家公司的文书工作！

blocks.html_en: Of course, most developers and technically skilled people know that computers aren’t magic and are very aware of the shortcomings. When you write code (by hand or using a coding agent) that accidentally deletes the production database of your company, “it’s the machine that did it” isn’t an excuse your manager will accept. And even in the age of coding agents, maintaining complicated software infrastructure is still hard work.

sentences.en: Of course, most developers and technically skilled people know that computers aren’t magic and are very aware of the shortcomings.
sentences.zh: 当然，大多数开发人员和技术熟练的人都知道计算机并不神奇，并且非常清楚其缺点。

sentences.en: When you write code (by hand or using a coding agent) that accidentally deletes the production database of your company, “it’s the machine that did it” isn’t an excuse your manager will accept.
sentences.zh: 当您编写的代码（手动或使用编码代理）意外删除了公司的生产数据库时，“是机器干的”并不是您的经理会接受的借口。

sentences.en: And even in the age of coding agents, maintaining complicated software infrastructure is still hard work.
sentences.zh: 即使在编码代理时代，维护复杂的软件基础设施仍然是一项艰巨的工作。

blocks.html_en: However, right now all over the world companies are firing their development teams and replacing them with AI agents, expecting everything will be the same, but cheaper. Of course, it’s not.

sentences.en: However, right now all over the world companies are firing their development teams and replacing them with AI agents, expecting everything will be the same, but cheaper.
sentences.zh: 然而，现在世界各地的公司都在解雇他们的开发团队，并用人工智能代理取代他们，期望一切都一样，但更便宜。

sentences.en: Of course, it’s not.
sentences.zh: 当然，事实并非如此。

blocks.html_en: It seems that for some people, it takes firing their developers to discover that machines are not the same as people, and code isn’t magic.

sentences.en: It seems that for some people, it takes firing their developers to discover that machines are not the same as people, and code isn’t magic.
sentences.zh: 似乎对于某些人来说，只有解雇他们的开发人员后，他们才会发现机器与人不同，而且代码并不神奇。

blocks.html_en: Leveraging our biggest strengths

sentences.en: Leveraging our biggest strengths
sentences.zh: 发挥我们最大的优势

blocks.html_en: Code and AI aren’t magic. And I think that we, as Wikimedians, are particularly well-placed to explain and show how the ‘magic’ works. Just as Wikipedia articles explain that things are usually a lot more complicated than you think.

sentences.en: Code and AI aren’t magic.
sentences.zh: 代码和人工智能并不是魔法。

sentences.en: And I think that we, as Wikimedians, are particularly well-placed to explain and show how the ‘magic’ works.
sentences.zh: 我认为，作为维基媒体人，我们特别有能力解释和展示“魔法”是如何运作的。

sentences.en: Just as Wikipedia articles explain that things are usually a lot more complicated than you think.
sentences.zh: 正如维基百科文章所解释的那样，事情通常比您想象的要复杂得多。

blocks.html_en: And that isn’t the only strength that we have. Wikimedia may be the David to big tech’s Goliath, but we often underestimate our own strengths.

sentences.en: And that isn’t the only strength that we have.
sentences.zh: 这并不是我们唯一的优势。

sentences.en: Wikimedia may be the David to big tech’s Goliath, but we often underestimate our own strengths.
sentences.zh: 维基媒体可能是大型科技巨头歌利亚的大卫，但我们经常低估自己的优势。

blocks.html_en: Even though the big tech companies that make the major LLMs have a seemingly limitless supply of money, they lack one thing that our community has in spades: trust and reliability. Wikimedians are fervent nitpickers, making sure statements are properly referenced and factually accurate. Even though LLMs tend to get many things right (because they have been trained on sources like Wikipedia) they also get many things wrong. Even if Google’s “AI overview” is wrong “only” 10% of the time, that means millions of people get wrong answers every day.

sentences.en: Even though the big tech companies that make the major LLMs have a seemingly limitless supply of money, they lack one thing that our community has in spades: trust and reliability.
sentences.zh: 尽管获得主要法学硕士学位的大型科技公司似乎拥有无限的资金供应，但他们缺乏我们社区所拥有的一件事：信任和可靠性。

sentences.en: Wikimedians are fervent nitpickers, making sure statements are properly referenced and factually accurate.
sentences.zh: 维基媒体人都是狂热的吹毛求疵者，确保声明得到正确引用并且事实准确。

sentences.en: Even though LLMs tend to get many things right (because they have been trained on sources like Wikipedia) they also get many things wrong.
sentences.zh: 尽管法学硕士往往会做对很多事情（因为他们接受过维基百科等来源的培训），但他们也会做错很多事情。

sentences.en: Even if Google’s “AI overview” is wrong “only” 10% of the time, that means millions of people get wrong answers every day.
sentences.zh: 即使谷歌的“人工智能概述”“仅”在 10% 的情况下是错误的，这也意味着每天都有数百万人得到错误的答案。

blocks.html_en: Wikipedia is the critical data set used in most LLMs. We need to figure out how we can take advantage of that. Our open licenses are both one of our biggest strengths and weaknesses. It’s very hard to make big tech pony up for our data in a capitalist world because they already got it for free. However, Wikimedia data is valuable because it’s one of the few high quality human-generated data sets (and probably less destructive than AI companies destroying print books to train their models).

sentences.en: Wikipedia is the critical data set used in most LLMs.
sentences.zh: 维基百科是大多数法学硕士使用的关键数据集。

sentences.en: We need to figure out how we can take advantage of that.
sentences.zh: 我们需要弄清楚如何利用这一点。

sentences.en: Our open licenses are both one of our biggest strengths and weaknesses.
sentences.zh: 我们的开放许可证既是我们最大的优势之一，也是我们的劣势之一。

sentences.en: It’s very hard to make big tech pony up for our data in a capitalist world because they already got it for free.
sentences.zh: 在资本主义世界中，很难让大型科技公司为我们的数据付费，因为他们已经免费获得了这些数据。

sentences.en: However, Wikimedia data is valuable because it’s one of the few high quality human-generated data sets (and probably less destructive than AI companies destroying print books to train their models).
sentences.zh: 然而，维基媒体数据很有价值，因为它是为数不多的高质量人类生成的数据集之一（而且可能比人工智能公司销毁纸质书籍来训练模型的破坏性要小）。

blocks.html_en: Another strength is that we are non-personalized. Folks using social media to get their news stay in their bubble, fed only the things that suit their taste. But on Wikipedia everyone reads the same article. Us not providing a ‘personalized reading experience’ is a feature, not a bug.

sentences.en: Another strength is that we are non-personalized.
sentences.zh: 另一个优势是我们不个性化。

sentences.en: Folks using social media to get their news stay in their bubble, fed only the things that suit their taste.
sentences.zh: 人们使用社交媒体来获取新闻，但他们仍沉浸在自己的泡沫中，只吃适合自己口味的东西。

sentences.en: But on Wikipedia everyone reads the same article.
sentences.zh: 但在维基百科上，每个人都读同一篇文章。

sentences.en: Us not providing a ‘personalized reading experience’ is a feature, not a bug.
sentences.zh: 我们不提供“个性化阅读体验”是一个功能，而不是一个错误。

blocks.html_en: We have the moral upper hand when we’re talking about big tech vs Wikimedia. Efforts like Grokipedia, which is fully AI-generated, fail because there are no humans to check on articles. Grokipedia cited the Kremlin as a prominent source on the invasion of Ukraine because they’re using AI models. A Wikimedian would spot that immediately.

sentences.en: We have the moral upper hand when we’re talking about big tech vs Wikimedia.
sentences.zh: 当我们谈论大型科技与维基媒体时，我们在道德上占据上风。

sentences.en: Efforts like Grokipedia, which is fully AI-generated, fail because there are no humans to check on articles.
sentences.zh: 像完全由人工智能生成的 Grokipedia 这样的努力失败了，因为没有人来检查文章。

sentences.en: Grokipedia cited the Kremlin as a prominent source on the invasion of Ukraine because they’re using AI models.
sentences.zh: Grokipedia 引用克里姆林宫作为入侵乌克兰的重要消息来源，因为他们正在使用人工智能模型。

sentences.en: A Wikimedian would spot that immediately.
sentences.zh: 维基媒体人会立即发现这一点。

blocks.html_en: AI is not magic, but you know what is? Consensus building with humans.

sentences.en: AI is not magic, but you know what is?
sentences.zh: 人工智能不是魔法，但你知道什么是魔法吗？

sentences.en: Consensus building with humans.
sentences.zh: 与人类建立共识。

blocks.html_en: Every Wikimedian should be a toolmaker

sentences.en: Every Wikimedian should be a toolmaker
sentences.zh: 每个维基媒体人都应该是工具制造者

blocks.html_en: We have identified our strengths. Now, how should we use them?

sentences.en: We have identified our strengths.
sentences.zh: 我们已经确定了我们的优势。

sentences.en: Now, how should we use them?
sentences.zh: 现在，我们应该如何使用它们？

blocks.html_en: It’s tempting to take a defensive stance against the big tech companies, and maybe even AI in general. But it’s better to play offense than defense. Big tech also doesn’t know what’s going to happen. It’s better if we try to invent the future ourselves instead of waiting around until something happens.

sentences.en: It’s tempting to take a defensive stance against the big tech companies, and maybe even AI in general.
sentences.zh: 人们很容易对大型科技公司甚至整个人工智能采取防御立场。

sentences.en: But it’s better to play offense than defense.
sentences.zh: 但进攻比防守更好。

sentences.en: Big tech also doesn’t know what’s going to happen.
sentences.zh: 大型科技公司也不知道会发生什么。

sentences.en: It’s better if we try to invent the future ourselves instead of waiting around until something happens.
sentences.zh: 如果我们尝试自己创造未来，而不是等到事情发生，那就更好了。

blocks.html_en: That means that right now we should focus on experiment over decisions. It’s better to do a lot of small experiments instead of making large-scale long-term bets. We should act deliberately, not emotionally, in the way Wikimedians do best: with nuance, knowledge and a scientific, objective look. And because of that we might be able to apply new technologies in a meaningful and useful way instead of jumping on the AI hype wagon and trying to cram AI into everything.

sentences.en: That means that right now we should focus on experiment over decisions.
sentences.zh: 这意味着我们现在应该专注于实验而不是决策。

sentences.en: It’s better to do a lot of small experiments instead of making large-scale long-term bets.
sentences.zh: 与其进行大规模的长期押注，不如进行大量的小实验。

sentences.en: We should act deliberately, not emotionally, in the way Wikimedians do best: with nuance, knowledge and a scientific, objective look.
sentences.zh: 我们应该按照维基媒体人最擅长的方式谨慎行事，而不是情绪化：细微差别、知识和科学、客观的眼光。

sentences.en: And because of that we might be able to apply new technologies in a meaningful and useful way instead of jumping on the AI hype wagon and trying to cram AI into everything.
sentences.zh: 正因为如此，我们也许能够以一种有意义且有用的方式应用新技术，而不是跳上人工智能炒作的马车并试图将人工智能塞进一切事物中。

blocks.html_en: Another reason why we should experiment now is because the current situation is not going to last forever. Using LLMs today can be dirt cheap because of the influx of venture capital. If something like Claude Opus or Fable is too expensive, DeepSeek v4-flash is almost as capable and can generate millions of tokens for next to nothing. To put that into perspective: the total codebase of MediaWiki with all extensions is roughly 3 million lines of code. An amount of code like that could be generated by this model for about 11 dollars.

sentences.en: Another reason why we should experiment now is because the current situation is not going to last forever.
sentences.zh: 我们现在应该进行试验的另一个原因是，目前的情况不会永远持续下去。

sentences.en: Using LLMs today can be dirt cheap because of the influx of venture capital.
sentences.zh: 由于风险资本的涌入，如今使用法学硕士的成本非常低。

sentences.en: If something like Claude Opus or Fable is too expensive, DeepSeek v4-flash is almost as capable and can generate millions of tokens for next to nothing.
sentences.zh: 如果像 Claude Opus 或 Fable 这样的东西太贵，那么 DeepSeek v4-flash 几乎同样有能力，并且可以几乎免费生成数百万个代币。

sentences.en: To put that into perspective: the total codebase of MediaWiki with all extensions is roughly 3 million lines of code.
sentences.zh: 客观地说：MediaWiki 及其所有扩展的总代码库大约有 300 万行代码。

sentences.en: An amount of code like that could be generated by this model for about 11 dollars.
sentences.zh: 该模型可以生成大约 11 美元的大量代码。

blocks.html_en: It’s very unlikely the situation will remain like this. The AI bubble will burst at some point in the near future, and then usage will suddenly be a lot more expensive. This also means that we need to prepare for that, and make sure that the tools we build don’t rely on AI models or can use simpler, self-hosted ones.

sentences.en: It’s very unlikely the situation will remain like this.
sentences.zh: 这种情况不太可能持续下去。

sentences.en: The AI bubble will burst at some point in the near future, and then usage will suddenly be a lot more expensive.
sentences.zh: 人工智能泡沫将在不久的将来的某个时候破裂，然后使用成本会突然变得更加昂贵。

sentences.en: This also means that we need to prepare for that, and make sure that the tools we build don’t rely on AI models or can use simpler, self-hosted ones.
sentences.zh: 这也意味着我们需要为此做好准备，并确保我们构建的工具不依赖人工智能模型，或者可以使用更简单的自托管模型。

blocks.html_en: It also gives us a great opportunity. As mentioned, people who can’t code suddenly can code now. And people who used to code in the past may rediscover their joy of coding again. They should get accustomed to the best practices that are evolving right now.

sentences.en: It also gives us a great opportunity.
sentences.zh: 这也给了我们一个很好的机会。

sentences.en: As mentioned, people who can’t code suddenly can code now.
sentences.zh: 如前所述，突然不会编码的人现在可以编码了。

sentences.en: And people who used to code in the past may rediscover their joy of coding again.
sentences.zh: 过去曾经编码的人可能会再次重新发现编码的乐趣。

sentences.en: They should get accustomed to the best practices that are evolving right now.
sentences.zh: 他们应该习惯目前正在发展的最佳实践。

blocks.html_en: • Using a coding agent. Claude Code is the most well-known but there are many capable open source alternatives as well like pi.dev and Hermes.

sentences.en: Using a coding agent.
sentences.zh: 使用编码剂。

sentences.en: Claude Code is the most well-known but there are many capable open source alternatives as well like pi.dev and Hermes.
sentences.zh: Claude Code 是最著名的，但也有许多功能强大的开源替代品，例如 pi.dev 和 Hermes。

blocks.html_en: • Be aware of the dangers. A coding agent can be run in ‘yolo mode‘, which means it has unrestricted access to your machine, up to and including deleting files by accident. You should either be careful in giving permissions or use a “harness” to restrict access to your system.

sentences.en: Be aware of the dangers.
sentences.zh: 注意其中的危险。

sentences.en: A coding agent can be run in ‘yolo mode‘, which means it has unrestricted access to your machine, up to and including deleting files by accident.
sentences.zh: 编码代理可以在“yolo 模式”下运行，这意味着它可以不受限制地访问您的计算机，甚至包括意外删除文件。

sentences.en: You should either be careful in giving permissions or use a “harness” to restrict access to your system.
sentences.zh: 您应该谨慎授予权限或使用“安全带”来限制对系统的访问。

blocks.html_en: • Use skills. Skills are text files written in Markdown that instruct a LLM about a specific task like ‘connecting to the Wikidata API’ or ‘finding pageview metrics on Wikipedia articles’.

sentences.en: Use skills.
sentences.zh: 使用技能。

blocks.html_en: • Use best practices. One thing that has always been very hard in software development is making sure people follow best practices. This includes things like unit tests and documentation, but it also includes providing your app in different languages (internationalization or ‘i18n’) and making sure it’s accessible (‘a11y’). With coding agents this becomes much easier. They don’t complain about writing documentation!

blocks.html_en: The Wikimedia Foundation announced that they are experimenting with hosting some open weights models on their LiftWing infrastructure. Currently, this includes the relatively modest Qwen 3-14B and 3.6-27B models. Hopefully those models will be more capable in future.

Blog archives

2026 年 7 月 30 日

人工智能不是魔法，但建立共识才是。 维基媒体 2026 年之后的未来 25 年笔记。

本文约 3,000 字，阅读起来大约需要 15 分钟。

1997 年，加里·卡斯帕罗夫 (Garry Kasparov) 在一场国际象棋比赛中输给了 IBM 制造的国际象棋计算机“深蓝”(Deep Blue)。 这是国际象棋卫冕世界冠军第一次输给电脑。

媒体将其描述为“人与机器”。 但深蓝的主要设计师徐凤雄后来写道，这种假设是错误的。 他将这场比赛视为一种人类与另一种人类的对抗。 人类作为表演者（卡斯帕罗夫）与人类作为工具制造者（深蓝团队）。

自从我上周从巴黎参加维基百科回来后，我一直在思考这场比赛：世界上最大的维基媒体人（维基百科及其兄弟姐妹的编写者）聚会。 今年有 1,250 人亲自参加，2,000 多人在线参加，我们通过为期五天的激烈演讲、研讨会以及与来自世界各地的维基人的许多会议和对话来庆祝维基百科的 25 岁生日。

几乎每一次会议和对话都贯穿着一个问题：在人工智能正在重塑数字世界和物理世界的世界中，我们作为一个社区如何应对它？ 正如 Christophe Henner 今年早些时候所写，人工智能不是一种工具，而是一种范式转变。 我们如何确保我们在未来 25 年继续发挥重要作用？

我从事维基媒体工作 21 年，同时也是一名开发人员。 过去几年，我在许多项目中使用了人工智能。 所以我对此有一些想法。

今年早些时候，我在米兰的维基媒体黑客马拉松期间举办了两场关于这个问题的研讨会，最终产生了这篇博文。 在维基百科，我在维基人工智能预会期间重复了这个研讨会。

在我组织了三场研讨会和五天的维基百科之后，我清楚了一件事：就像卡斯帕罗夫与其他人类而不是机器比赛一样，我们正在与其他人类竞争，他们已经找到了如何在我们所做的一些事情上做得更好。

这意味着什么？ 我们也应该成为更好的工具制造者。

Unsure of what all the terms in this article mean? Click here to read a glossary of terms.
  • 这些项目是指维基媒体项目（维基百科、维基数据、维基共享资源等）。
  • 社区、运动或维基媒体人是从事这些项目的人，无论是受雇（例如来自维基媒体基金会或附属机构）还是志愿者。
  • 基金会或 WMF 是指维基媒体基金会，它是为维基媒体项目提供托管和技术基础设施的支持组织。
  • 附属机构指的是当地维基媒体分会（例如荷兰维基媒体）和用户组（例如 LGBT+ 用户组）。
  • LLM 是“大型语言模型”，因此 ChatGPT、Claude、Gemini 等。
  • 前沿模型是为上面列出的最著名的 LLM 聊天机器人提供支持的人工智能模型。
  • 本地模型是在您自己的计算机上而不是在云中运行的模型。 这些模型的能力通常不如前沿模型，但足以胜任特定任务。 能力更强的本地模型需要大量 RAM； 16GB 通常是最低限度。
  • 开放权重模型可以免费下载，并且可以在您自己的计算机上运行（与许多封闭的前沿模型相比）。 然而，一些功能更强大的模型可能需要大量 RAM，以至于它们仍然在云中运行（例如 DeepSeek V4 Pro 需要 862GB RAM）。
  • 推理是使用法学硕士生成内容，例如使用 LLM 聊天机器人编写代码。
  • 令牌是法学硕士作为输入并产生作为输出的基本单位。 大多数模型都是根据代币定价的，更好的模型往往每个代币的成本更高。
  • 开放许可证是维基媒体项目上的内容可用的条件。 Creative Commons BY-SA 和 Zero 是最受欢迎的。 开放许可证意味着您可以免费将内容重复用于大多数用途，甚至可以用于商业用途。
  • Markdown 是法学硕士的重要输入/输出格式。 它是一种纯文本格式，提供可转换为 HTML 的简单语法。 例如。 *星号*之间的文本以斜体呈现。

三大挑战

作为一场运动，我们面临三大挑战：

1. 人类减少

我们的社区依赖于参观我们项目的人们。 因为我们需要新的编辑，他们从读者开始。 我们需要捐款。 这些项目的资金大部分来自路过的读者的小额捐款。 如果由于人们通过法学硕士或谷歌的“人工智能概述”使用维基百科内容而导致该来源枯竭，我们就会遇到问题。

维基媒体基金会已经注意到读者人数下降是一个真实的趋势。 有趣的是，一些类似的项目，如 OpenStreetMap，并不那么依赖读者，并且始终更注重成为数据源而不是目的地。 所以也许这并不像我们想象的那么严重。 但就目前而言，我想说，我们应该谨慎行事，并将读者人数下降视为一个严重的问题。

我们的项目中人员减少的另一个后果是，我们内容的消费者和内容制作者之间的距离会变得更大。 向人们解释这些文章是由真实的人类共同撰写的，这一直是一个问题。 法学硕士可能会让人们认为维基百科只是一群写文章的人工智能机器人。 他们可能对捐赠或成为编辑犹豫不决的另一个原因。

2. 更多机器人

当人类访问我们的项目越来越少时，机器人却越来越多地出现。 其中许多机器人都是刮刀，以不可持续的速度收集我们的数据。 这给我们的基础设施带来了巨大的压力。 感觉就像是双输的局面。 维基媒体为法学硕士提供了最重要的数据源之一，作为回报，我们得到了大量的抓取机器人，我们需要在基础设施上投入更多。

3. 更多的污渍

人工智能生成的文章也是一个问题。 除了我们一直以来经常遇到的破坏行为外，现在我们还需要处理看似写得很好的文章，而这些文章实际上是由法学硕士撰写的。

我们一直都包含机器生成的内容（一些维基百科甚至几乎完全用机器生成的内容编写），问题是在包含人工智能生成的内容方面划清界限。

这不仅仅是一个内部问题。 维基百科依赖参考文献来撰写可验证的文章。 如果互联网变成了人工智能污水的污水池，那么找到可靠的来源就会变得越来越难。

内部斗争

还有一些内部问题可能会削弱我们的地位。

组织米兰研讨会的一个重要原因是，并非运动中的所有声音都被听到。 我们是否应该使用人工智能，或者完全禁止使用法学硕士和编码代理？ 尤其是年轻人可能会对人工智能的任何使用持非常负面的看法。 如果我们社区的部分人感觉被排除在这场讨论之外，可能会导致内部两极分化。

有足够的理由怀疑或反对人工智能的使用。 前面提到的问题包括使用我们数据的公司缺乏互惠、能源消耗、某些模型被“微调”的恶劣工作条件、工作岗位流失、人工智能为军事“杀手无人机”提供动力、可疑的政府关系等等。

然而，令人惊讶的是，巴黎关于这个话题的讨论却很少。 也许人们已经简单地接受了人工智能将成为一项重要技术的未来？ 或者也许他们没有，但他们没有说话？ 我不知道，但我很想阅读或听到这些人的更多信息。

另一个问题是志愿者、附属机构和基金会之间运动中的微妙平衡。 这三个派系之间的关系很复杂，有时甚至非常紧张。 例如，请参阅有关董事会成员资格的拟议新规则、资助附属机构的结构更新以及基金会与维基工人联合团结工会相关的行动（或者更确切地说缺乏行动）。 重要的决定可能会因内部辩论和讨论而被推迟和阻碍。

人类必须承担责任

让我们回到“人作为表演者与人作为工具制造者”的叙述。

如果我们同意世界上的重大转变不是“机器正在接管”，而是“人类控制的机器正在接管”，那么人类必须对他们建造和使用的机器的行为负责也是有道理的。

这似乎是显而易见的，但事实并非如此。 以前依赖程序员的人们现在突然可以自己做很多事情了。 这可能感觉就像魔法一样。 突然间，他们能够编写复杂的 Excel 公式！ 或者，vibecode 是一个小应用程序，用于处理他们以前必须雇用一家公司的文书工作！

当然，大多数开发人员和技术熟练的人都知道计算机并不神奇，并且非常清楚其缺点。 当您编写的代码（手动或使用编码代理）意外删除了公司的生产数据库时，“是机器干的”并不是您的经理会接受的借口。 即使在编码代理时代，维护复杂的软件基础设施仍然是一项艰巨的工作。

然而，现在世界各地的公司都在解雇他们的开发团队，并用人工智能代理取代他们，期望一切都一样，但更便宜。 当然，事实并非如此。

似乎对于某些人来说，只有解雇他们的开发人员后，他们才会发现机器与人不同，而且代码并不神奇。

发挥我们最大的优势

代码和人工智能并不是魔法。 我认为，作为维基媒体人，我们特别有能力解释和展示“魔法”是如何运作的。 正如维基百科文章所解释的那样，事情通常比您想象的要复杂得多。

这并不是我们唯一的优势。 维基媒体可能是大型科技巨头歌利亚的大卫，但我们经常低估自己的优势。

尽管获得主要法学硕士学位的大型科技公司似乎拥有无限的资金供应，但他们缺乏我们社区所拥有的一件事：信任和可靠性。 维基媒体人都是狂热的吹毛求疵者，确保声明得到正确引用并且事实准确。 尽管法学硕士往往会做对很多事情（因为他们接受过维基百科等来源的培训），但他们也会做错很多事情。 即使谷歌的“人工智能概述”“仅”在 10% 的情况下是错误的，这也意味着每天都有数百万人得到错误的答案。

维基百科是大多数法学硕士使用的关键数据集。 我们需要弄清楚如何利用这一点。 我们的开放许可证既是我们最大的优势之一，也是我们的劣势之一。 在资本主义世界中，很难让大型科技公司为我们的数据付费，因为他们已经免费获得了这些数据。 然而，维基媒体数据很有价值，因为它是为数不多的高质量人类生成的数据集之一（而且可能比人工智能公司销毁纸质书籍来训练模型的破坏性要小）。

另一个优势是我们不个性化。 人们使用社交媒体来获取新闻，但他们仍沉浸在自己的泡沫中，只吃适合自己口味的东西。 但在维基百科上，每个人都读同一篇文章。 我们不提供“个性化阅读体验”是一个功能，而不是一个错误。

当我们谈论大型科技与维基媒体时，我们在道德上占据上风。 像完全由人工智能生成的 Grokipedia 这样的努力失败了，因为没有人来检查文章。 Grokipedia 引用克里姆林宫作为入侵乌克兰的重要消息来源，因为他们正在使用人工智能模型。 维基媒体人会立即发现这一点。

人工智能不是魔法，但你知道什么是魔法吗？ 与人类建立共识。

每个维基媒体人都应该是工具制造者

我们已经确定了我们的优势。 现在，我们应该如何使用它们？

人们很容易对大型科技公司甚至整个人工智能采取防御立场。 但进攻比防守更好。 大型科技公司也不知道会发生什么。 如果我们尝试自己创造未来，而不是等到事情发生，那就更好了。

这意味着我们现在应该专注于实验而不是决策。 与其进行大规模的长期押注，不如进行大量的小实验。 我们应该按照维基媒体人最擅长的方式谨慎行事，而不是情绪化：细微差别、知识和科学、客观的眼光。 正因为如此，我们也许能够以一种有意义且有用的方式应用新技术，而不是跳上人工智能炒作的马车并试图将人工智能塞进一切事物中。

我们现在应该进行试验的另一个原因是，目前的情况不会永远持续下去。 由于风险资本的涌入，如今使用法学硕士的成本非常低。 如果像 Claude Opus 或 Fable 这样的东西太贵，那么 DeepSeek v4-flash 几乎同样有能力，并且可以几乎免费生成数百万个代币。 客观地说：MediaWiki 及其所有扩展的总代码库大约有 300 万行代码。 该模型可以生成大约 11 美元的大量代码。

这种情况不太可能持续下去。 人工智能泡沫将在不久的将来的某个时候破裂，然后使用成本会突然变得更加昂贵。 这也意味着我们需要为此做好准备，并确保我们构建的工具不依赖人工智能模型，或者可以使用更简单的自托管模型。

这也给了我们一个很好的机会。 如前所述，突然不会编码的人现在可以编码了。 过去曾经编码的人可能会再次重新发现编码的乐趣。 他们应该习惯目前正在发展的最佳实践。

Want to know what those best practices are? Click here to find out.
  1. 使用编码剂。 Claude Code 是最著名的，但也有许多功能强大的开源替代品，例如 pi.dev 和 Hermes。
  2. 注意其中的危险。 编码代理可以在“yolo 模式”下运行，这意味着它可以不受限制地访问您的计算机，甚至包括意外删除文件。 您应该谨慎授予权限或使用“安全带”来限制对系统的访问。
  3. 使用技能。 技能是用 Markdown 编写的文本文件，指导法学硕士执行特定任务，例如“连接到维基数据 API”或“在维基百科文章上查找页面浏览量指标”。
  4. 尝试不同的模型。 显然每个人都应该尝试前沿模型，但如果只是为了练习，尝试本地托管或开放权重模型也是很有趣的。
  5. 使用最佳实践。 在软件开发中一直非常困难的一件事是确保人们遵循最佳实践。 这包括单元测试和文档等内容，还包括以不同语言（国际化或“i18n”）提供应用程序并确保其可访问（“a11y”）。 有了编码代理，这变得更加容易。 他们不会抱怨编写文档！

维基媒体基金会宣布，他们正在尝试在其 LiftWing 基础设施上托管一些开放权重模型。 目前，这包括相对温和的 Qwen 3-14B 和 3.6-27B 型号。 希望这些模型将来能够变得更加强大。

当然，“我们应该做什么”的答案比“构建大量工具”更微妙。 我们已经拥有 4,000 多个工具，其中许多没有维护和/或损坏。 我们不想获得过多的新工具，而这些工具随后就不再维护且不再使用。 我们可能需要对我们使用的工具设定更高的期望，或者在弃用和删除旧工具时更加警惕。

将人工智能用于维基媒体并不意味着撰写文章

那么，如果每个维基媒体人都构建工具，那么我们构建什么？ 当谈论生成人工智能时，首先想到的是“写文章”，但这可能是最无用的应用程序之一。 正如维基媒体人除了撰写维基百科文章之外还做更多事情一样，人工智能也可以用于许多不同的应用程序。

我喜欢 Andrew Lih 谈论 Wiki AI 工具的“摩擦矩阵”。 一个轴（对于人类）的负担低/高，而另一轴的影响低/高。 看看具有高影响力但低负担的工具是很有趣的。 这意味着维基人完成的许多繁琐的重复任务可以通过构建新的人工智能辅助工具来取代或至少简化。

Ada Homolova 和 Johan Schuijt 展示的 PoliLoom 工具就是一个很好的例子。 它允许将来自维基百科的有关政客的事实导入到他们的维基数据项目中。 这包括出生地和政治立场等数据点。 他们使用人工智能分析维基百科文章以突出显示句子（例如“Jane Doe 出生于巴黎”）并准备适当的维基数据编辑（例如 Jane Doe -> Born in Paris）。 始终需要人工编辑来验证建议的编辑。 这是人类可以完成的任务的一个很好的例子，但人工智能可以加速这一任务。

人工智能工具的另一个明显用例是帮助较小的语言社区。 维基百科有近 350 个语言版本。 对于他们中的许多人来说，维基百科是该语言的唯一主要参考书。 人工智能工具可以帮助参与这些版本的数量有限的志愿者维护他们的项目。

组队

当然，我们作为维基人，在这段旅程中并不孤单。 我们一直有很多朋友与我们分享关于开放数据访问、可验证性和维护开放网络的价值观。 这包括互联网档案馆、知识共享、OpenStreetMap 等各方。 只有与这些各方合作，共同商定我们应该采取哪些步骤，以确保互联网始终符合我们的愿景，才有意义。

因此，很高兴看到像 Mosaic 这样的举措，它汇集了许多不同的“公共”相关方，尤其是因为画廊、图书馆、档案馆和博物馆 (GLAM) 等知识和文化机构的可能性是巨大的。 人们只能想象这样一种未来：GLAM 使用新的人工智能工具轻松地将相关数据共享到维基媒体。

我喜欢的新工具的一个建议是 Audrey Tang 关于“LLM 编辑按钮”的想法。 每个编辑都是从在每篇维基百科文章顶部的某个时刻发现“编辑”按钮开始的。 随着从网络上使用维基媒体内容到法学硕士的转变，我们缺少这个按钮。 人工智能时代的“编辑”按钮会是什么样子？

我们可以共同创造一个替代由大型科技公司主导的商业封闭网络的方案。 人类保持控制并建立一个每个人都可以自由分享所有知识总和的世界。

维基百科生日快乐！
